# 190 Ostomy Construction and Management Personalizing the Stoma for the Patient

## Indications for Stomas
- Created as a temporary means of fecal diversion for high-risk anastomoses.
- Created as permanent orifices for the passage of stool or urine when surgical resection prohibits the body’s normal orifices from accomplishing these tasks.

## Permanent Colostomies
- Usually created from the sigmoid or descending colon.
- Typically associated with distal bowel resection.
- Colostomies proximal to the splenic flexure function poorly, are difficult to manage, and are at high risk for complications.
- If transverse or ascending colon is contemplated, strongly consider resecting remaining large bowel and creating an end ileostomy.

## Table 190.1: Common Indications for Permanent Colostomy

::: {.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- Rectal cancer
- Radiation proctopathy
- Incontinence
- Refractory anorectal infection

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
- Ischemia
- Crohn’s disease
- Diverticular disease
- Sacral decubitus

:::
:::



## Permanent Ileostomies
- Less common currently due to the development and acceptance of ileal pouch–anal anastomosis (IPAA).
- Created for inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), familial adenomatous polyposis, multiple synchronous colorectal cancers, colonic dysmotility, and miscellaneous disorders.
- Poor anal function, comorbid diseases, or quality of life considerations may make an ileostomy preferable to complex reconstructive options.

## Temporary Diverting Stomas
- Created in association with distal bowel resections when anastomosis is unsafe.
- Used to protect a distal anastomosis when operative conditions or comorbidities make proximal diversion prudent.
- Three predominant types: end sigmoid colostomy, loop colostomy, and loop ileostomy.

## Preoperative Considerations: Patient Preparation
- Patients undergoing elective or emergency surgery with possible stoma creation require adequate preoperative preparation.
- Emergent surgery dictates rapid preparation, but stoma considerations must not be neglected.
- Many patients lack knowledge of intestinal stomas; preoperative education by the surgeon combined with printed material is very helpful.

## Role of Wound Ostomy Care Nurse (WOCN)
- All patients should meet with a WOCN or enterostomal therapist (ET) if available.
- Provides specific information regarding stoma appliances, dietary and clothing alterations, and pouch management.
- Most importantly, helps select the appropriate abdominal wall site for the future stoma.
- Preoperative counseling and marking by an ET improves postoperative quality of life.

## Peer Support and Stoma Groups
- Patients scheduled for stomal surgery benefit from meeting or speaking with other ostomates.
- Patients adjusted to life with a stoma provide an excellent, non-medical source of information.
- Local chapters of the United Ostomy Association of America and the Crohn’s and Colitis Foundation are valuable resources.

## Preoperative Stoma Site Marking
- Patients should have their stoma site marked prior to surgery.
- An abdominal surgeon should be able to locate and mark stoma sites.
- Marking is simple, straightforward, and requires only a few minutes.

## Figure 190.1: The Ostomy Triangle
- Defined by three abdominal wall landmarks:
  - Anterior superior iliac spine
  - Pubic tubercle
  - Umbilicus
- The stoma should lie within this triangle overlying the rectus muscle, generally at the site of an infraumbilical bulge.

## Stoma Siting Principles
- Site should be located on a flat segment of the abdominal wall.
- Must be 5 cm away from bony prominences, the umbilicus, prior surgical scars, or skin folds.
- Patient should sit up after marking to ensure new skin folds do not interfere.
- Patient’s beltline should be identified and avoided to decrease postoperative clothing restrictions.

## Special Circumstances: Obesity and Wheelchair Patients
- Obese individuals: A large pannus may preclude stoma placement below the umbilicus. The pannus is thicker here and may hide the stoma, making management difficult.
- Wheelchair patients: Should be marked while in their chair to avoid unanticipated postoperative difficulties.
- Despite restrictions, the stoma should pass through the rectus abdominal muscle to decrease complications of parastomal hernia and stomal prolapse.

## Operative Techniques: End Stomas Overview
- End ileostomies are routinely performed in association with partial or total colorectal resections.
- Exposure is generally through a midline incision.
- Stoma is created after performing the indicated bowel resection.

## End Ileostomy: Skin and Fascia Preparation
- The premarked stoma site (usually right lower quadrant) is excised.
- A skin disc the size of a quarter is removed, sparing all subcutaneous fat to support the stoma postoperatively.
- Fat is separated with cautery to expose the anterior rectus sheath.

## Figure 190.2: Skin Disc Excision
- Visualizes the excision of a disc of skin at the stoma site.
- Demonstrates preservation of subcutaneous fat for postoperative support.

## Figure 190.3: Anterior Rectus Sheath Opened
- Shows the anterior rectus sheath opened vertically with cautery for 3 to 4 cm.

## Figure 190.4: Stoma Site Admits Two Fingers
- Rectus abdominis muscle is split in the direction of its fibers to expose the posterior sheath.
- Posterior sheath is opened with cautery.
- The defect is enlarged to admit two fingers.

## End Ileostomy: Bowel Preparation
- Residual retroperitoneal attachments are divided to facilitate passage of the bowel through the abdominal wall without tension.
- Mesentery may be cleared from the terminal 5 to 6 cm of the ileum.
- Care is taken to leave at least a 1-cm strip of mesentery with the ileum to carry a vessel paralleling the ileal wall, preventing stomal ischemia.

## Figure 190.5: Ileum Prepared
- Illustrates the preparation of the ileum for ileostomy creation.
- Highlights the preservation of the 1-cm mesenteric strip to prevent ischemia.

## End Ileostomy: Maturation and Eversion
- Ileum is oriented with the cut mesenteric edge cephalad and passed through the abdominal wall defect.
- Ileum should protrude 5 to 6 cm beyond skin level and appear pink and well perfused.
- Lateral ileal gutter may be closed to prevent small bowel obstruction (suturing free edge of mesentery to abdominal wall lateral to midline incision up to falciform ligament).
- No need to suture ileum to posterior fascia (does not decrease risk of prolapse or hernia).

## Figure 190.6: Tripartite Bites
- Tripartite sutures contain:
  1. Dermis
  2. Sero-muscular layer of the bowel at the fascial level
  3. Full-thickness bites of the cut edge of the ileum
- Three or four everting sutures are placed at the ordinals without tying.
- General traction facilitates eversion; enterocutaneous anastomosis is completed with additional sutures (4-8) approximating bowel mucosa to dermis.

## Left-Sided End Colostomies
- Usually created in association with distal colorectal resection.
- Lateral attachments of the colon are transected along the white line of Toldt until sufficient colon is mobilized.
- Colostomy must protrude from the abdominal wall and be matured without tension.
- Premarked site is usually in the lower left quadrant; cutaneous and fascial openings may need to be slightly larger.

## End Colostomy Maturation
- Colon is oriented without twisting and passed through the abdominal wall.
- Should protrude beyond abdominal skin and appear well perfused.
- Careful attention to the edge of the mesentery to prevent tearing.
- No need to close lateral gutter or suture colon to posterior abdominal fascia.
- Alternatively, a retroperitoneal colostomy can be created (tunneling under posterolateral peritoneum), associated with decreased rates of parastomal herniation and prolapse.

## Modified Technique for Thick Abdominal Wall
- Meagher et al. devised a technique for end sigmoid colostomy in patients with a thick abdominal wall.
- A small wound protector is inserted into the stoma trephine and opened maximally.
- Bowel is passed through the wetted/lubricated wound protector.
- Inner ring is transected and removed; remaining protector is brought out externally.
- Decreases spillage and minimizes bowel trauma during exteriorization, particularly in obese patients.

## Loop End Stoma Variation
- Useful in obese patients or those with shortened or thickened mesentery.
- Difficult to get stoma or mesentery to reach skin without tension, or blood supply may be questionable.
- A distal loop of bowel is selected; using umbilical tape or large red rubber for traction, the loop end is brought through the abdominal wall without dividing the mesentery.
- A stomal rod helps maintain traction; bowel is matured as in a traditional loop stoma.

## Figure 190.7: Creation of a Loop End Stoma
- Visualizes the creation of a loop end stoma.
- Shows the use of traction to bring the loop end through the abdominal wall without dividing the mesentery.

## Loop Stomas Overview
- Created to divert the fecal stream away from the "downstream" intestine.
- Three types: loop ileostomy, loop colostomy, and end loop stomas.
- Transverse loop colostomy was historically common but is poorly tolerated with high complication rates; largely replaced by loop ileostomy.
- Diverting colostomy may be safer if relieving distal obstruction and the ileocecal valve is competent (prevents closed loop obstruction).

## Loop Ileostomy Creation
- Generally created in association with distal bowel resection.
- Most distal segment of terminal ileum that reaches abdominal wall without tension is selected (15 to 30 cm proximal to ileocecal valve or ileoanal reservoir).
- Ileum is encircled with a Penrose drain or umbilical tape after ensuring mobility.
- Abdominal wall defect created as for end ileostomy (may need to be slightly larger).
- Proper orientation is ensured; distal end is marked with a suture to prevent maturation of the incorrect segment.

## Loop Ileostomy Maturation
- Ileal loop passed through abdominal wall without twisting; protrudes 4 to 5 cm beyond skin.
- Distal aspect of ileum just above abdominal wall is transected along approximately 80% of its circumference (from mesentery to mesentery).
- Distal end matured with simple sutures between full-thickness terminal bowel and dermis.
- Proximal end is everted using three tripartite bites, tied with gentle traction applied within the lumen.
- Maturation completed with two additional sutures between dermis and full thickness of terminal ileum.

## Figure 190.8: Loop Ileostomy with Support Rod
- A 4- to 5-cm loop of distal ileum is brought through abdominal aperture with no twist.
- A stoma rod is passed through the mesentery.
- The ileum is opened toward the nonfunctioning limb and a tripartite suture is placed.
- The rod is sutured to the skin and the remainder of the ileostomy is matured with sutures.

## Loop Sigmoid Colostomy
- Created to prevent fecal stream from reaching rectum and anus in cases of incontinence, severe anorectal infection, or for proximal protection after complex anal reconstruction or distal obstruction.
- Created in identical fashion to loop ileostomy, but commonly placed in the left lower quadrant.
- Eversion is not strictly necessary due to the noncaustic nature of the effluent from the left colon.
- End loop or divided loop stoma is often easier to create and functions better.

## End Loop Stomas: Overview and Benefits
- Three types: end loop ileostomy, end loop colostomy, and end loop ileocolostomy.
- Three main benefits:
  1. Make stoma management easier postoperatively (appear similar to end stomas).
  2. Can be created with remote sections of the intestine (e.g., end loop ileotransverse colostomy).
  3. Do not require formal laparotomy for stoma takedown.

## End Loop Ileostomy Creation
- Following intestinal resection and abdominal wall defect creation:
- Small defect created in mesentery at preselected ileal stomal site.
- Bowel transected with linear stapling device.
- Proximal (functional) end brought through abdominal wall as for standard end ileostomy.
- Nonfunctional segment can be brought through fascia and sutured to functional bowel limb or Scarpa fascia (completely diverts bowel).
- Alternatively, antimesenteric corner of distal nonfunctional bowel brought through same stoma site, transected, and matured to abdominal wall without eversion.
- Proximal bowel everted and matured; single suture connects proximal and distal segments.

## Figure 190.9: Creation of an End Loop Ileostomy
- Abdomen explored through midline incision; ostomy opening created.
- Segment of ileum selected and divided with linear cutting stapler.
- Divided ends brought through ostomy aperture (functional end marked with suture).
- Staples of functional end excised, bowel matured producing a 2-cm spout.
- Staples at antimesenteric end of nonfunctioning end excised; small end sutured to deep dermis and medial edge of functioning stoma.

## End Loop Colostomy Creation
- Created with a preselected segment of the sigmoid colon.
- Mobilized appropriately and passed through previously created abdominal wall defect similar to end loop ileostomy.
- Abdominal incision closed appropriately.
- End colostomy matured similarly to end loop ileostomy.
- Proximal end may be everted, but a flush colostomy may also be created.

## End Loop Ileocolostomy Creation
- Performed in association with resection of the right colon when anastomosis is unsafe.
- Terminal ileum prepared as for routine end ileostomy.
- Stoma site often created in right upper quadrant to facilitate passage of ileostomy and distal transverse colon through the same aperture.
- Terminal ileum brought through abdominal wall.
- Stapled-off end of proximal transverse colon brought through the same defect.
- Antimesenteric corner of transverse colon staple line transected and matured without eversion.
- Terminal ileum matured as for standard end ileostomy; final suture connects transverse colon and ileum.

## Figure 190.10: Creation of an End Loop Ileocolostomy
- Abdomen explored via midline incision.
- Terminal ileum and right colon are resected.
- Functional end of ileum and end of nonfunctional colon are brought through the ostomy aperture.
- Ostomy is matured similarly to the end loop ileostomy.

## Laparoscopic Stomas: General Principles
- Can be created laparoscopically if needed in conjunction with laparoscopic bowel resection or as an isolated procedure.
- Principles applying to open ileostomy creation also apply laparoscopically.
- Site selected according to patient’s body habitus and functional needs.
- If colectomy is essential, ileostomy siting should be considered at trocar placement.
- Trocar can be placed through future stoma trephine, but sites adjacent to trephine within the footprint of the stoma appliance should be avoided.

## Laparoscopic Ileostomy Technique
- Terminal ileum located just proximal to ileocecal valve; followed retrograde until a segment easily reaching the abdominal wall is identified.
- Pneumoperitoneum should be deflated when assessing ileal length.
- Proper loop of bowel grasped with grasper through stoma trephine; proximal and distal bowels carefully identified.
- Pneumoperitoneum released; stoma trephine created in standard fashion around the grasper.
- Loop eviscerated carefully without twisting.
- Limited pneumoperitoneum reestablished to confirm proper orientation (essential to avoid creating ileostomy from distal limb).
- Stoma matured in standard fashion.

## Laparoscopic Colostomy Technique
- Sigmoid colostomy is most common.
- If trocars placed for rectosigmoid resection, no additional ports needed.
- If performed without other abdominal surgery, three or four ports may be necessary (camera at umbilicus, two in right mid-abdomen and right lower quadrant, fourth through marked stoma site if mobilization required).
- Sigmoid and descending colon mobilized if no resection performed.
- Pneumoperitoneum released to check for length; distal end marked.
- Pneumoperitoneum decompressed; stoma trephine created; colon brought through without twisting and matured.

## Modified Abdominoplasty (Abdominal Wall Contouring)
- Beneficial for patients with stomal retraction (e.g., continent ileostomies, dense adhesions, short gut), prolapse, large peristomal hernias, abdominal wall laxity (major weight loss), or peristomal skin problems like pyoderma gangrenosum.
- Technique similar to plastic surgery: low curvilinear transverse incision at inferior abdominal fold or 2 to 3 cm above pubis and anterior superior iliac spines.
- Flap of skin and subcutaneous tissue created by electrocautery dissection cranially, just above fascia.
- Perforating vessels identified and ligated or cauterized.

## Figure 190.11: Modified Abdominoplasty
- Addresses redundant abdominal wall folds of skin associated with ileostomy retraction.
- Frontal view and sagittal section demonstrating skin and subcutaneous fat incisions.
- Excess skin and subcutaneous fat excised.
- Ileostomy relocated through upper flap and skin incisions closed.
- Closed-suction drains placed below flaps.

## Medial Approach for Abdominal Wall Modification
- Incision through midline incision down to fascia.
- Dissection carried laterally just above fascia until stoma is reached.
- Ostomy dissected free of skin and subcutaneous tissue.
- Lateral dissection to flanks provides laxity to advance previous stoma site to midline (advancement flap).
- New ostomy opening created in fresh skin; excess fat excised; redundant midline skin resected.
- If skin flap not redundant enough, subcutaneous fat can be excised and stoma returned to original skin opening through thinned flap.

## Figure 190.12: Medial Approach
- Frontal view with skin incisions marked.
- Cross section demonstrating midline incision and areas of subcutaneous fat excision.
- After removal of excess subcutaneous tissue, incision is closed, flaps attached to fascia, and stoma matured with adequate eversion.

## Liposuction for Stomal Retraction
- Rapid and significant weight gain in ostomy patients may produce stomal retraction.
- If weight loss attempts fail and stomal revision is not desirable or feasible (e.g., continent ileostomy, short gut), liposuction is an excellent option.
- Preferred if no associated stomal stenosis or hernia.
- Experienced plastic surgeons carefully remove subcutaneous fat around the stoma, leaving a flat smooth peristomal skin surface.
- Removed fatty tissue will not be redeposited despite additional weight gain.

## Antiadhesion Barriers and Stomas
- Some authors advocate using carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) and sodium hyaluronate (Seprafilm) when creating temporary loop stomas to facilitate ostomy reversal.
- Wrapping the ileum at stoma creation minimizes adhesions between stoma and abdominal wall, making takedown easier.
- Technique: Loop eviscerated, sheet of CMC cut in half. Proximal and distal limbs of bowel and adjacent mesentery wrapped in a "sushi roll" style.
- Loop brought through abdominal wall and matured in standard fashion.

## Enterostomal Therapy: Role of WOCN/ET
- Dedicated WOCN or ET’s contribution to long-term quality of life is immeasurable.
- Provide preoperative counseling, early postoperative education, and act as long-term resource.
- Supply information on appliance choices, local support groups, dietary/clothing modifications, and aid in managing skin problems, parastomal hernias, prolapse, and other complications.
- Surgeon must ensure patient is educated in appliance management if ET support is unavailable.

## Appliance Management
- Appliance must be emptied frequently to avoid overfilling and dislodgement.
- Ileostomies: usually emptied 4 to 6 times per day.
- Colostomies: emptied once or twice per day, or once every other day.
- Entire appliance changed every 4 to 7 days.
- Pouches should generally be changed when stoma is least active (often after a period of fasting) to avoid controlling fresh output during the procedure.

## Table 190.2: Stoma Care Steps
1. Gather all supplies.
2. Clean stoma and peristomal skin with water; pat dry. Shave or clip peristomal hair if indicated.
3. Gently remove soiled pouch by pushing down on skin while lifting up on pouch. Discard in odor-proof plastic bag.
4. Use stoma-measuring guide or established pattern to determine size. Cut-to-fit pouch: trace pattern and cut opening to match.
5. Apply skin barrier paste or skin sealant to skin. Allow to dry.
6. Remove paper backing from pouch or barrier, center pouch opening over stoma, press into place, and attach closure.

## Managing Gas and Odor
- Major concerns for most ostomates.
- Gas sources: swallowed air and bacterial breakdown of ingested foodstuffs (particularly carbohydrates).
- Minimize swallowed air: avoid straws, excessive talking while eating, chewing gum, and smoking.
- Common gas-producing foods: beans, broccoli, onions, Brussels sprouts, beer, dairy (in lactose-deficient individuals).
- Odor reducers: yogurt, parsley, orange juice, odor-proof pouches, charcoal filters, pouch deodorants, orally ingested deodorants (bismuth subgallate, chlorophyllin complex).
- Most important key: good peristomal hygiene and creating a leak-proof seal.

## Complications: Overview and Incidence
- Complications after stoma creation remain extremely common (10% to 70% depending on study methodology, follow-up length, and definition).
- Early complications (within 1 month): peristomal skin irritation, leakage, high output, ischemia.
- Late complications (more than 1 month): parastomal hernia, prolapse, obstruction, stenosis.
- Park et al. (20-year review): 34% incidence (28% early, 6% late). Skin irritation most common early (12%) and late (6%).
- Duchesne et al.: 25% overall complication rate. Ileostomies had higher complication rates than colostomies. Sixfold decrease in complications when ET was involved.

## Skin Irritation and Leakage
- Most common early local complication.
- Far more common in ileostomy patients due to liquid, caustic effluent.
- Preventable with preoperative marking by ET, appropriate location, and careful appliance fitting.
- Monitor for allergic reactions to appliance components.
- Older patients with eyesight/dexterity limitations and obese patients are at higher risk.
- Avoid creams/ointments that interfere with appliance adherence.
- Downsize appliance at first postoperative visit as stoma becomes less edematous and abdomen less distended.

## Figure 190.13: Skin Irritation
- Illustrates skin irritation around the stoma site from a poorly fitting appliance.
- Highlights the importance of proper siting and secure fit to minimize noxious, irritating effects of leakage.

## High-Output Stomas
- Typically described in association with ileostomy rather than colostomy.
- Marked diarrhea and dehydration occur in 5% to 20% of ileostomy patients, greatest risk in early postoperative period (3rd to 8th day).
- Output peaks on 4th postoperative day (up to 3.2 L reported).
- Effluent is rich in sodium; hyponatremia can be a problem.
- Managed by oral rehydration (sports drinks). Patients with previous bowel resection or Crohn’s disease may require parenteral hydration and nutrition.
- Clostridium difficile enteritis is an increasingly reported cause of ileostomy diarrhea, especially after total colectomy for IBD.

## Bowel Obstruction and Food Bolus
- 23% of patients with an ileostomy ultimately develop bowel obstruction.
- Adhesions are most common cause; small bowel volvulus or internal hernia may be culprits.
- Suturing mesentery to lateral abdominal wall has not been shown to prevent volvulus or obstruction.
- Food bolus obstruction: accumulation of poorly digested foodstuffs (popcorn, peanuts, fresh fruits/vegetables).
- Treatment: red rubber catheter gently inserted into ostomy with saline irrigation until obstruction is relieved.

## Ischemia
- Edema and venous congestion are very common after stoma creation due to mechanical trauma and compression of small mesenteric venules.
- Ischemia may be related to tension on the mesentery or excessive mesenteric division (especially in obese patients or emergency surgery).
- Common error: dividing sigmoidal vessels to obtain length for colostomy. Instead, divide inferior mesenteric vessels proximally and/or mobilize splenic flexure.
- If ischemia is apparent, insert glass test tube or flexible endoscope. If viable at fascial level, observe. If questionable, immediate laparotomy and revision required.

## Parastomal Hernia
- Most common stoma complication requiring operative intervention.
- Develops in 2% to 28% of end ileostomies and 4% to 48% of end colostomies.
- Risk factors: obesity, advanced age, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
- Preventive measures: smallest possible opening without causing ischemia. Prophylactic prosthetic mesh (underlay position) may reduce risk.
- Surgical correction results have historically been poor (high recurrence). Mesh repairs (0%-33% recurrence) are superior to primary repair (46%-100%) or stoma relocation (76%).
- Intraperitoneal or underlay mesh repair (Sugarbaker technique) has encouraging results.

## Figure 190.14: Large Parastomal Hernia
- Visual representation of a large parastomal hernia.
- Demonstrates the significant abdominal wall defect and protrusion associated with this common late complication.

## Stenosis
- May result from ischemia, excessive tension, retraction, or recurrent IBD.
- Reported incidence typically less than 10%.
- Mild asymptomatic stenosis requires no treatment.
- Skin-level stenosis treated with local procedures (Z- or W-plasty).
- Crohn’s disease-associated stenosis usually requires formal bowel resection.
- Timing of surgery is important: allow acute inflammatory response to subside with temporizing measures (convex pouch, gentle digital dilation) to facilitate local revision later.

## Prolapse
- Risk of stoma prolapse reported to be 11.8% at 13 years.
- Transverse loop colostomies are especially notorious for prolapse; the efferent limb is virtually always the offending cause.
- Mesenteric fixation or lateral space closure do not appear to reduce incidence.
- Asymptomatic prolapse requires no treatment, especially if temporary.
- Surgical intervention warranted if prolapse causes ischemia, obstruction, or pouching problems.
- Incarcerated prolapse without advanced ischemia: sugar can be applied as a desiccant to facilitate reduction.

## Figure 190.15: Prolapsed Ileostomy
- Shows a prolapsed ileostomy.
- Highlights the elongation and protrusion of the bowel segment through the stoma site.

## Figure 190.16: Large Prolapse of Transverse Loop Colostomy
- Illustrates a large prolapse of a transverse loop colostomy.
- Demonstrates why loop ileostomy is commonly preferred over loop colostomy for temporary fecal diversion.

## Peristomal Varices
- May cause life-threatening hemorrhage.
- Occur at the mucocutaneous border due to anastomoses between the high-pressure portal venous system and low-pressure subcutaneous veins of the abdominal wall.
- Suspected in ostomates with serious liver disease (e.g., extensive liver metastases, sclerosing cholangitis).
- Confirmed by typical purplish hue or "caput medusae" of peristomal skin (visible only after removing stoma wafer).
- Acute bleed management: local pressure with epinephrine-soaked gauze or suture ligation.
- Additional therapy: lowering portal pressure (TIPS, percutaneous coil embolization).
- Long-term success may require liver transplantation or mucocutaneous disconnection/stomal relocation.

## Figure 190.17: Peristomal Varices
- Shows the characteristic blue hue of peristomal varices.
- This presentation is visible only after removing the stoma appliance, highlighting the need for careful skin inspection in at-risk patients.

## Summary and Conclusion
- Successful ostomy construction requires meticulous preoperative planning, including ET involvement and precise stoma siting.
- A variety of operative techniques (end, loop, end loop, laparoscopic) allow for personalization based on patient anatomy and clinical scenario.
- Enterostomal therapy is critical for long-term quality of life and complication prevention.
- Early recognition and appropriate management of complications (skin irritation, high output, obstruction, ischemia, hernia, stenosis, prolapse, varices) are essential for optimal patient outcomes.
